q: Which flame colour is given by potassium compounds?
x: Potassium gives a lilac flame. Golden yellow is sodium, crimson red is lithium (or strontium) and brick red is calcium.

q: Which Group 2 metal does not react with water or steam, even at red heat?
x: Beryllium is the least reactive Group 2 metal and does not react with water even as steam. Magnesium reacts with steam (and slowly with hot water), while calcium and barium react with cold water; reactivity rises down the group.

q: Alkaline earth metals are harder and have higher melting points than the alkali metals of the same period. The main reason is that:
o: Each atom gives two electrons to the sea of electrons, so the metallic bonding is stronger
Their atoms are joined by covalent bonds
x: Group 2 atoms release two valence electrons each and form smaller, doubly charged cations, so the metallic bonding is stronger. Their atoms are smaller and their ionisation energies are higher than those of Group 1.

q: Equal masses of magnesium and calcium are each added to excess dilute hydrochloric acid. What is the ratio of the volume of hydrogen from magnesium to that from calcium, measured under the same conditions? (Mg = 24, Ca = 40)
x: Both react as M + 2HCl → MCl₂ + H₂, so moles of H₂ equal moles of metal. For mass m: m/24 : m/40 = 40 : 24 = 5 : 3. Inverting the ratio gives 3 : 5; equal masses are not equal moles, so 1 : 1 is wrong.

q: Lithium has the most negative standard electrode potential of the alkali metals, even though its first ionisation energy is the highest in the group. The main reason is that:
o: Lithium has the largest atoms in the group
Lithium has the lowest melting point in the group
Li⁺ ions are not hydrated in water
The very small Li⁺ ion has a very large hydration energy
x: The electrode potential reflects the whole change M(s) → M⁺(aq). The small Li⁺ ion is very strongly hydrated, and this large release of energy outweighs its higher ionisation energy. Lithium has the smallest atoms and the highest melting point in the group.

q: Which Group 2 oxide is the most basic?
x: Basic character of Group 2 oxides increases down the group as the metal becomes more electropositive, so BaO is the most basic of these (it gives the strong base Ba(OH)₂). MgO is only weakly basic.

q: The thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates increases from MgCO₃ to BaCO₃. The best explanation is that, down the group:
o: The cations become smaller and more highly charged
The larger cations have lower polarising power and distort the carbonate ion less
x: A small cation such as Mg²⁺ polarises the large CO₃²⁻ ion, weakening a C–O bond so CO₂ is lost easily. Larger cations further down the group polarise it less, so the carbonate must be heated more strongly. All are +2 ions and the carbonate ion is the same throughout.

q: 0.10 mol of calcium nitrate is heated strongly until it has decomposed completely, as other Group 2 nitrates do. What total volume of gas is given off, measured at STP? (molar volume 22.4 dm³)
x: 2Ca(NO₃)₂ → 2CaO + 4NO₂ + O₂, so 0.10 mol gives 0.20 mol NO₂ and 0.05 mol O₂, a total of 0.25 mol = 0.25 × 22.4 = 5.6 dm³. Counting only NO₂ gives 4.48 dm³; counting only O₂ gives 1.12 dm³.

q: The solubility of Group 2 sulphates decreases from MgSO₄ to BaSO₄. The main reason is that, down the group:
o: The hydration energy of the cation falls faster than the lattice energy, which changes little because the sulphate ion is large
The charge on the cation increases
x: With the large SO₄²⁻ ion, a bigger cation hardly changes the lattice energy, but the hydration energy of the cation falls steadily as it gets larger. Less energy is released on dissolving, so solubility falls. The charge stays +2 throughout.

q: Magnesium carbonate is heated strongly. Besides carbon dioxide, which product is formed?
x: MgCO₃ → MgO + CO₂: Group 2 carbonates decompose to the metal oxide and carbon dioxide. No hydrogen is present, so a hydroxide cannot form, and the metal is not set free.

q: In the Nelson cell for the manufacture of sodium hydroxide from brine, which gases are given off at the electrodes?
o: Hydrogen at the graphite anode, chlorine at the steel cathode
Chlorine at the graphite anode, hydrogen at the steel cathode
Oxygen at the graphite anode, hydrogen at the steel cathode
Chlorine at the graphite anode, oxygen at the steel cathode
x: Cl⁻ ions from the concentrated brine are oxidised at the anode to chlorine; water is reduced at the cathode to hydrogen, leaving OH⁻ that forms NaOH with Na⁺. Swapping the electrodes is the common slip.

q: A Downs cell produces 23 kg of sodium. What volume of chlorine, measured at STP, is produced at the same time? (Na = 23; molar volume 22.4 dm³)
x: 2NaCl → 2Na + Cl₂. 23 kg of Na is 1000 mol, which comes with 500 mol Cl₂ = 500 × 22.4 = 11 200 dm³. Forgetting the 2 : 1 ratio gives 22 400 dm³.

q: Lime mortar, a paste of slaked lime, sand and water, slowly hardens in air. The main reaction is:
x: Slaked lime in the mortar absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and turns into hard calcium carbonate as the water evaporates. CaO + H₂O is the earlier slaking step, and the gypsum reaction belongs to plaster, not lime mortar.

q: Why is a small amount of gypsum added to cement clinker when cement is ground?
o: To slow down the setting of the cement
To make the cement set within seconds
To give the cement its grey colour
To lower the melting point of the clinker
x: Gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) acts as a retarder: without it the cement would set too quickly to be worked. It is added after the clinker is made, so it does not affect the kiln.

q: Which alkali metal carbonate decomposes into its oxide and carbon dioxide when heated in a Bunsen flame?
x: The very small Li⁺ ion polarises the carbonate ion, so Li₂CO₃ → Li₂O + CO₂ on heating, like MgCO₃ (a diagonal likeness). The other alkali metal carbonates are stable at Bunsen temperatures.

q: The main reason for the anomalous behaviour of lithium compared with the other alkali metals is its:
o: Very small atomic and ionic size, which gives Li⁺ a high polarising power
x: The tiny Li atom and Li⁺ ion give a high charge density, so lithium's compounds are more covalent and its behaviour resembles magnesium. Lithium has the smallest radius and the highest ionisation energy in the group, and it forms only Li⁺.

q: Beryllium has a diagonal relationship with which element, so that both form covalent chlorides and amphoteric oxides?
x: Be (group 2, period 2) and Al (group 13, period 3) lie diagonally, and their ions have similar charge densities: both give covalent chlorides that act as Lewis acids and amphoteric oxides and hydroxides. Magnesium is Be's group neighbour, not its diagonal partner.

q: A solution of beryllium chloride in water is acidic. The best explanation is that:
o: Be²⁺ ions combine with OH⁻ ions taken from the air
The small, highly polarising Be²⁺ ion pulls electron density from its bound water molecules, so [Be(H₂O)₄]²⁺ releases H⁺
Chloride ions react with water to give HCl and OH⁻
Beryllium chloride is oxidised by water to give chlorine
x: Be²⁺ is tiny and doubly charged, so it strongly polarises the O–H bonds of the water molecules bound to it: [Be(H₂O)₄]²⁺ + H₂O ⇌ [Be(H₂O)₃(OH)]⁺ + H₃O⁺. Cl⁻ is the ion of a strong acid and does not hydrolyse, so the chloride option is wrong.
